abduction.short_description: Places linked to reported alien abductions, where people say they were taken aboard a craft or lost hours they cannot account for.

accused.short_description: People accused of witchcraft, marked where they lived, were tried or met their end.

amphitheatre-site.short_description: Sites of Roman amphitheatres where little or nothing now stands above ground.

amphitheatre.short_description: Surviving Roman amphitheatres, the arenas where crowds gathered for gladiator fights and public spectacles.

ancient-road.short_description: Stretches of ancient road, mostly Roman, where the original surface or line can still be seen.

ancient-tree.short_description: Data reproduced with the permission of The Woodland Trust.

apotropaic.short_description: Marks and carvings made to ward off evil, such as witch marks, votive crosses and devil's doors, often found in old churches.

aqueduct.short_description: Ancient aqueducts, mostly Roman, built to carry water across valleys to towns and cities.

arthurian.short_description: Places tied to the legends of King Arthur, from his court to the caves where he is said to sleep.

balancing-rock.short_description: Rocks balanced improbably on top of others. Some can be rocked by hand, and many were said to have been placed by giants.

barrow.short_description: Prehistoric burial mounds of earth or stone raised over the dead.

battle.short_description: If you're looking for ghosts - a battlefield is a good place to start (currently only battles before 1900 are included). Be sure to read the history and tune into what each side was fighting for!

big-cat.short_description: Sightings of mysterious big cats roaming the countryside, far from anywhere they should live.

black-eyed.short_description: Encounters with black-eyed children: pale youngsters with completely black eyes who knock and ask to be let in.

blowhole.short_description: Sea caves with an opening above, where the waves force water and spray up through the rock.

bullaun.short_description: Bullaun stones: boulders with bowl-shaped hollows, often found at early Irish church sites. The rainwater they collect is said to cure.

burial.short_description: Ancient cemeteries and burial grounds, such as Saxon cemeteries.

beehive-tomb.short_description: Beehive (tholos) tombs: circular stone burial chambers roofed with a corbelled dome, best known from Mycenaean Greece.

chambered-cairn.short_description: Neolithic chambered cairns: stone burial mounds containing passages and chambers for the dead.

cairn.short_description: Cairns: piles of stones raised as burial monuments or landmarks.

canine.short_description: Phantom dogs and hounds, from spectral black dogs and hellhounds to faithful spirits.

cartoquirk.short_description: Quirks of the map itself, such as Null Island at 0°, 0° and the points halfway between the equator and the poles and halfway around the world.

cave.short_description: Natural caves, many with legends, ghosts or a long history of human use.

celtic-cross.short_description: Celtic crosses: stone crosses with a ring around the intersection, carved in early medieval Britain and Ireland.

clootie-tree.short_description: Clootie wells and trees, where strips of cloth are tied to the branches as offerings. As the rag rots away, so the ailment is said to fade.

coffin-rest.short_description: Coffin rests: stones or ledges on old corpse roads where the bearers set down the coffin on the way to the churchyard.

crater.short_description: Craters blasted out by meteorite impacts, some now filled by lakes.

crossroads-burial.short_description: Graves at crossroads, where suicides and suspected witches were once buried away from consecrated ground. Many are said to be haunted.

cup-and-ring.short_description: Cup-and-ring marks: prehistoric rock carvings of hollows and concentric rings whose meaning is still unknown.

curse.short_description: Places with a curse attached, from cursed buildings and families to blighted land, and the tales of how they came to be.

cyclopean.short_description: Cyclopean masonry features massive, irregular stone blocks fitted so precisely that ancient Greeks believed only the mythical Cyclopes could have built them.

dark-sky.short_description: Dark-sky places: parks, reserves and sanctuaries protected from light pollution, ideal for stargazing.

demon.short_description: Tales of demons: evil spirits that tempt, torment or strike bargains with mortals.

devil.short_description: Places where the Devil is said to have walked, struck bargains or left his mark.

devils-bridge.short_description: Bridges said to have been built by the Devil, usually in exchange for the soul of the first to cross.

dolmen.short_description: Dolmen are single chambered megalithic tomb. Upright stones support a large 'table' stone.

e-book.short_description: E-Books covering specific geographic areas. If you buy a linked book, we may earn a commission from Bookshop.org, whose fees support independent bookshops!

earthworks.short_description: Archaeological earthworks are man-made landscape features created by the deliberate movement or shaping of soil, such as ditches, mounds, or banks. Where the purpose of the structures is not known they are simply titled 'earthworks'

egyptian-sarcophagus.short_description: Museums holding ancient Egyptian sarcophagi and mummy cases.

erratic.short_description: Stones transported by glaciers over 25000 years ago

event.short_description: Festivals and events with a pagan, folkloric or occult theme.

exhibit.short_description: Museums and exhibits of the strange, from witchcraft and magic to the paranormal and curious objects.

fairy.short_description: Fairy folklore: places where the fair folk were seen, stole away mortals or left their mark.

fairy-tree.short_description: Fairy trees, usually lone hawthorns, which it is bad luck to cut or harm.

folk-song.short_description: Places that gave their name or story to traditional folk songs.

changeling.short_description: In folklore, a changeling is a fairy child left in place of a human infant, taken out of love or belief that the human child is exceptionally beautiful or destined for a life of wonder. In reality, the changeling myth was often a tragic explanation for infants born with (at the time) unexplained illnesses, such that parents sometimes resorted to cruel superstitions in an attempt to 'drive out' the fairy imposter.

dragon.short_description: Dragon legends: places where dragons and winged serpents were said to live, terrorise the locals and be slain.

folklore-cat.short_description: Cats of folklore and legend, such as the immortal cat of Chipping Sodbury.

folklore-fox.short_description: Fox spirits of folklore, such as the Japanese kitsune and the white foxes of Inari shrines.

folklore-giant.short_description: Giants of folklore, and the places they built, threw, fought over or lie buried beneath.

folklore-humanoid.short_description: Humanoid creatures of folklore that are neither quite human nor ghost.

folklore-serpent.short_description: Serpents and great worms of legend.

folklore-vampire.short_description: Vampires of folklore and the places they are said to haunt.

troll.short_description: Trolls: large, menacing creatures of Norse and British folklore that lurk in hills and under bridges, and may turn to stone in daylight.

folklore.short_description: Local folklore and legends of every kind, from phantom beasts to strange customs.

folklore-swine.short_description: Pig-men and other swine creatures of folklore and modern legend.

folly.short_description: A folly is a decorative building constructed mainly for visual effect in a landscape or garden, often designed to look picturesque, exotic, or ruin-like and typically serving little or no practical purpose.

fortlet.short_description: Small Roman forts, including the milecastles and milefortlets of Hadrian's Wall.

fossil.short_description: Fossil sites, including petrified trees and fossil forests.

gallows.short_description: Gallows and gibbets: sites of hangings, where the bodies of the executed were often left on display.

general.short_description: A miscellany of curiosities that don't fit any other category.

geo-glyph.short_description: Geoglyphs: large figures cut into hillsides or laid out on the ground, like the chalk white horses of England and the Nazca lines.

geofold.short_description: Spectacular folds in rock, where ancient layers have been buckled and crumpled.

ghost-horse.short_description: Spectral horses, some of them omens of danger or death.

ghost-light.short_description: Ghost lights: unexplained glowing lights such as will-o'-the-wisps and corpse candles, said to foretell death or lead travellers astray.

ghost-photo.short_description: Places where a ghost is said to have been caught on camera.

ghost-ship.short_description: Phantom ships seen sailing where no ship should be, often as an omen of storms or disaster.

ghost-sign.short_description: Ghost signs: faded hand-painted adverts and signs surviving on old walls.

ghost-train.short_description: 'All Aboard...' Or should that be 'None Aboard'? Ghost trains tend to serve as reminders of tragedies long passed.

ghost-walk.short_description: Ghost walks and tours, where guides lead you through a place's haunted history.

giants-grave.short_description: Giants' graves (tombe dei giganti): Bronze Age collective tombs built by the Nuragic people of Sardinia.

grave.short_description: Individual graves with a story, from the resting places of famous mystics to graves bound up with prophecy and legend.

gravity-hill.short_description: Gravity hills, where an optical illusion makes cars and water appear to roll uphill.

grid.short_description: Points where whole-degree lines of latitude and longitude cross.

haunted-road.short_description: Haunted roads, where drivers report phantom figures, vehicles and animals.

haunted-stay.short_description: Haunted hotels, inns and guesthouses where you can stay the night.

haunting.short_description: Haunted places: buildings, roads and landscapes with reported ghosts.

headless-rider.short_description: Headless horsemen and other headless riders of legend.

henge.short_description: Henges: prehistoric circular earthworks with a bank and an inner ditch.

high-strangeness.short_description: Hotspots of 'high strangeness', where many kinds of unexplained phenomena are reported.

hill-fort.short_description: Hill forts: fortified hilltop enclosures, mostly from the Iron Age.

hoard.short_description: Places where buried hoards of coins, jewellery and other treasure were found.

hogback-grave.short_description: Hogback stones: Viking-age grave markers carved like longhouses with curved roofs, often guarded by beasts at each end.

holy-well.short_description: Holy wells: springs and wells associated with saints, healing and pilgrimage.

hominid.short_description: Sightings of wild ape-men and hairy hominids, from Bigfoot-like creatures to local beasts.

hum.short_description: Places plagued by 'the hum', a persistent low drone heard by some residents but never traced to a source.

i-spy.short_description: Fun things to look out for.

lazy-code.short_description: Glitches in the simulation: places so strange they suggest reality is running on lazy code, from twisted forests to boulders split perfectly in two.

legend.short_description: Traditional stories handed down about a place, part history and part embellishment, such as Pope Joan and the walled-up bride of Rozafa Castle.

lithiatric-mark.short_description: Usually downward grooves in the stonework - these marks are currently believed to be the result of material (dust) from the building being gathered for use in folk medicine.

lost-mine.short_description: Lost mines, whose rich seams were found once and never located again.

sunken-treasure.short_description: Treasure said to be lost beneath the water.

lost-treasure.short_description: Treasures said to lie buried or hidden, still waiting to be found.

manmade-cave.short_description: Man-made caves and tunnels, from chalk mines to the mysterious erdstall passages of central Europe.

marian-apparition.short_description: Places where the Virgin Mary is said to have appeared.

medicine-wheel.short_description: Medicine wheels: circles and lines of stones laid out by Indigenous peoples of the North American plains.

memento-mori.short_description: Memento mori carvings: skulls, crossbones and hourglasses reminding the living that they too will die.

merfolk.short_description: Mermaids and mermen: half-human, half-fish beings said to lure sailors to their doom and sometimes marry mortals.

milestone.short_description: Ancient milestones, mostly Roman, that marked distances along the roads.

mortsafe.short_description: Mortsafes: iron cages and frames set over graves to keep out body snatchers.

mothman.short_description: Mothman, the red-eyed winged creature reported around Point Pleasant, West Virginia, in 1966 and 1967.

motte-and-bailey.short_description: Motte-and-bailey castles: early Norman castles built as an earth mound with an enclosed courtyard beside it.

mummified-person.short_description: Mummified remains, including bog bodies and naturally preserved mummies.

mystery.short_description: Unsolved mysteries, such as puzzling inscriptions, cryptograms and messages.

myth-swine.short_description: Monstrous boars and swine of myth, such as the Erymanthian Boar captured by Heracles.

myth-touch.short_description: Places where myths have effected landscapes or other features still visible today.

name-dragon.short_description: Places whose names come from dragons, such as Dragonby and Dragon Hill.

name.short_description: Places with strange names, and the stories of how they got them.

named-ghost.short_description: Ghosts known by name, from grey ladies and green ladies to other famous spirits.

national-trust.short_description: National Trust properties: historic houses, gardens and landscapes cared for by the Trust.

nuraghe.short_description: The nuraghi are massive, beehive-shaped stone towers built between 1600 and 1200 BCE, unique to Sardinia and numbering more than 7000 across the island. Their exact purpose remains uncertain, but they likely served as fortresses, dwellings, temples, and symbols of power, forming the monumental legacy of the Nuragic civilisation.

occult-market.short_description: Markets selling witchcraft, magic and fetish goods.

occult-shop.short_description: Shops selling witchcraft, occult and esoteric supplies.

ossuary.short_description: Ossuaries and charnel houses, where the bones of the dead are stacked and displayed.

pagan.short_description: Places used for pre-Christian or modern pagan worship, such as altars and offering sites.

petroglyph.short_description: Petroglyphs: ancient images carved into rock.

petrosomatoglyph.short_description: Petrosomatoglyphs: marks in rock said to be the footprints or body prints of gods, saints or heroes.

plague-pit.short_description: Plague pits: mass graves of plague victims.

plague-stone.short_description: Holes in the stone were filled with vinegar in to 'sterilize' coins payed by plague sufferers

podcast.short_description: Podcasts exploring folklore and the strange.

podcast-episode.short_description: Podcast episodes about a particular place or tale.

point-zero.short_description: Mile Zero or Kilometer Zero - is a point in a city that distances to that city are measured from. So when a road sign says 'London 100 miles' it means its 100 miles to that spot!

possession.short_description: Cases where people were said to be taken over by a demon or spirit, often ending in exorcism.

practitioner.short_description: Witches, wizards, cunning folk and occultists: people who practised magic, and where they lived or worked.

prediction.short_description: Prophecies tied to a place: foretold disasters, omens and predictions waiting to come true.

public-bookcase.short_description: Public bookcases and little free libraries. Take a book, leave a book.

redwood.short_description: Native to California but making special appearances across the globe - it's the worlds largest tree!

research-org.short_description: Organisations that research psychical and paranormal phenomena.

revenant.short_description: Revenants: the dead who return to the world of the living.

rock-cut-tomb.short_description: Tombs carved into solid rock, such as the domus de janas ('fairy houses') of Sardinia.

ruined-castle.short_description: Ruined castles, from crumbling keeps to scattered foundations.

sacred-landscape.short_description: Natural landmarks, such as mountains and rock formations, held sacred by the people who live around them.

sacrificial-stone.short_description: Sacrificial stones: boulders with hollows where offerings were left, common in the Baltic and Nordic countries.

sacred-stone.short_description: Sacred stones: boulders venerated as places of offering, healing or worship.

sacred-tree.short_description: Sacred trees, venerated for their age, their spirit or their holy associations.

sacrificial-altar.short_description: Ancient altars and high places where sacrifices were made.

saint.short_description: Places tied to the lives and legends of saints.

sanctuary-stone.short_description: Sanctuary stones that marked the bounds of a church's right of sanctuary, within which a fugitive could claim protection.

scratch-dial.short_description: These medieval sundials are most often located on the south side of a church. Some dials are found on other walls too (including inside churches) probably due to rebuilding...

sea-monster.short_description: Large unknown creatures reported in seas and lakes, from Nessie in Loch Ness to the Turtle Lake Monster.

settlement.short_description: The remains of ancient towns and settlements, from Roman towns to the island city of Nan Madol.

sheela-na-gig.short_description: Sheela na gigs: medieval carvings of naked women displaying an exaggerated vulva, often found on churches.

ship-burial.short_description: Ship burials, where the dead were laid in a ship or boat beneath a mound.

simulacrum.short_description: Simulacra: rocks and landscapes that look like faces, figures or creatures.

site.short_description: Haunted places with a story attached.

spiritborne.short_description: People said to have been carried off by spirits, often to a churchyard.

runestone.short_description: Runestones: standing stones carved with runic inscriptions, mostly from the Viking age.

standing-stone.short_description: Standing stones: single upright stones, mostly raised in prehistory.

statue.short_description: Statues said to move, walk or bring misfortune to those who disturb them.

stone-circle.short_description: Stone circles: rings of standing stones raised in prehistory.

stopped-clock.short_description: Clocks stopped at the moment of a tragedy.

sub-street.short_description: Hidden streets and underground passages you can visit.

sunken-settlement.short_description: Villages drowned by reservoirs and lakes, whose remains sometimes reappear in dry summers.

temple.short_description: Ancient temples: buildings dedicated to gods, such as Roman temples to Mithras and Heracles.

the-drop.short_description: A notorious local spot of ill repute. You have been warned.

thin-place.short_description: Thin places, where the boundary between this world and the next is said to be thin.

timeslip.short_description: Places where people report briefly stepping into the past.

tower.short_description: Towers of the Knights Templar, and round churches modelled on the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.

tradition.short_description: Old local customs still kept alive, such as cheese rolling down a hillside or handing out bread and cheese to the parish.

tunnel.short_description: Secret tunnels and passages of legend.

ufo.short_description: Places where unidentified flying objects were reported, from single sightings to famous incidents with many witnesses.

uncontacted.short_description: Uncontacted peoples are indigenous groups living without sustained contact with the world community. There are thought to be between 100 and 200 such tribes.

unique.short_description: Places that are one of a kind, such as a church tower built askew or the smallest church in England.

unmarked-door.short_description: Hidden venues behind unmarked doors. Look for the sign that they're open.

urban-legend.short_description: Modern folk tales told as true, usually by someone who heard it from a friend of a friend, and pinned to a real place.

vile-vortex.short_description: Vile vortices: twelve points around the globe that Ivan Sanderson proposed as zones of disappearances and anomalies, like the Bermuda Triangle.

vitrified-fort.short_description: Vitrified forts: stone forts whose walls have been fused into glass by intense heat, by means still debated.

volcanic-columns.short_description: Columnar basalt: lava that cooled into giant hexagonal columns, like the Giant's Causeway.

vortex.short_description: Energy vortices, where some visitors feel spiritual or healing energy.

wayside-cross.short_description: Some crosses were erected in medieval times and travellers would pray at them for a safe journey; thus making their location an indicator of ancient routes.

webcam.short_description: Live webcams of wild and remote places.

weird.short_description: Places that are simply strange and fit no other category, such as churches that seem to vanish from view.

wishing.short_description: Trees where either coins are inserted (not recommended) or ribbons tied to mark wishes

witch.short_description: Witches of folklore: women and men said to cast spells, curse livestock and neighbours, or consort with the Devil.

witch-hunt-memorial-plaque.short_description: Memorial plaques to the people accused and executed in the witch hunts.

witch-hunt-memorial.short_description: Memorials to the people accused and executed in the witch hunts.

wizard.short_description: Wizards and sorcerers of legend: men said to command spirits, cast spells or outwit the Devil.
